highlight.text: The bodies of the two are posed so as to be evocative of passionate foreplay, while their faces remain impassive - a common theme in contemporary Safavid art.

work.text: At the time, Abbasi had already become known as a bold, innovative painter of drawings and album miniatures - a break from the traditional artistic establishment of Safavid Iran, which favored illustrations.
Embracing lovers are one of the themes of Riza's work after 1610, but he was equally fond of depicting old men, especially dervishes

moment.text: That these are of the time of Shah ‘Abbas I we know once more from the pages of Pietro della Valle, who considered them lascivious. They are in fact similar in style, though coarser in execution, than those of Riza-yi ‘Abbasi but are, from the point of view of the [20th] century, gently sentimental rather than provocative.

matters.text: Though the artist had previously painted the nude female figures, the introduction of a male figure in Lovers elevated the work from simply evoking erotic thoughts to outright representing courting.

Clouds, flowers, and trees are also present in the painting, serving to encircle the couple, while a carafe of wine and half-empty plate of fruit lies by their feet, implying some indulgence has already taken place.
